title: The Mosel
subtitle: Slate, slopes and Riesling
objectives: Describe the Mosel's slopes and soils

steps.title: Steep slate
steps.body: The Mosel winds through western Germany at about 50 degrees north, one of the coolest regions for quality wine. The best vineyards rise on steep, south-facing slopes above the river, some over 60 degrees, like the Bremmer Calmont. Dark slate soils absorb heat and the river reflects light, helping Riesling ripen.

steps.title: The Mosel style
steps.body: Mosel Riesling is light, often 7.5 to 10% alcohol, with high acidity, green apple, peach and floral notes. Many are off-dry or sweet, with sugar balancing fierce acidity. They age for decades. Working these slopes is mostly by hand and costs several times more than on flat land.

steps.prompt: Match each Mosel feature to its effect.
steps.explanation: Every feature helps a cool region ripen Riesling.

steps.body: A Mosel Kabinett at 8% alcohol is one of the best lunchtime wines in the world. Light, refreshing and great with spicy food.

steps.prompt: Why can Riesling ripen in a region as cool as the Mosel?
options: Steep south-facing slate slopes capture heat and light
steps.explanation: Slope, aspect, slate and the river all add warmth and light.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Mosel's steep slate slopes help Riesling ripen at 50 degrees north
Mosel Riesling is light, high in acidity and often off-dry
Its tributaries, the Saar and Ruwer, are even cooler
